units.mastery_criterion: Identifies the force and a controlled load; the prediction is diagnostic, not assumed entry mastery.
units.task: Use a diagram of a balanced beam with a marked pivot and two push positions. Identify the push and predict which position may need less effort; state what must be kept the same in a fair comparison.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can verbally trace the energy transformation in the flashlight from chemical to light.
units.task: Demonstrate energy transformations using a battery-powered fan and a flashlight. Trace the energy from chemical (battery) to electrical, to mechanical (fan) or light/heat (flashlight).

units.mastery_criterion: Student can verbally state the defining feature of at least three simple machines when prompted.
units.task: Introduce the six simple machines by displaying physical examples (a ruler for a lever, a spool for a wheel and axle, a doorstop for a wedge, a ramp for an inclined plane, a screw, and a basic pulley). Explain the defining characteristic of each group.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can verbally distinguish between a tangible object and an intangible process or knowledge.
units.task: Introduce the concepts of hard (tangible) and soft (intangible) technology by comparing a physical book (hard) to the story/rules inside it (soft), and a smartphone (hard) to its software (soft).

units.mastery_criterion: Student can explain what phantom load is and why unplugging devices saves energy.
units.task: Discuss 'phantom load' (energy consumed by devices plugged in but turned off). Analyze a scenario of a house left with everything plugged in while the family is on vacation.

units.mastery_criterion: Classifies the nutrient terms using the supplied record and allows several nutrient groups in one food.
units.task: Introduce macronutrients and micronutrients. Display printed images of 15 common foods and model how to sort them into categories based on their primary nutrient type and whether they are of animal or vegetal origin. Use multi-nutrient food records: a food may contain several nutrient types. Never classify the whole food as a single nutrient.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can identify the x-axis, y-axis, and title on the modeled graph.
units.task: Model how to draw a bar chart using a simple data table of food origins. Demonstrate labeling the x-axis and y-axis, choosing a scale, and drawing the bars to the correct height.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally list the three main steps of cultivation.
units.task: Outline the basic steps of plant cultivation on the board: soil preparation, sowing/transplanting, and care (watering, pest control). Discuss each step using images of a farm.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can explain what the colored water represents and why it is dangerous.
units.task: Explain the concept of cross-contamination. Use a simulated demonstration with a sponge (representing raw meat) soaked in colored water and a clean piece of plastic (representing bread) to show how germs transfer if the same knife/surface is used.

units.mastery_criterion: Identifies the zero/unit error and states a matching correction.
units.task: Inspect fictional diagrams of a model measured with a ruler and a scale. Find a missing unit or non-zero starting point, describe its effect on the record, and correct the recording procedure.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can define internal and external geological phenomena.
units.task: Explain the difference between internal geological phenomena (originating inside the Earth) and external phenomena (surface level). Show pictures of earthquakes, volcanoes, landslides, and rockfalls.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can describe the correct eye-level technique for reading a graduated scale.
units.task: Introduce the pluviometer. Show a large physical model or clear diagram of a graduated cylinder. Explain how to read the meniscus at eye level in millimeters.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can distinguish between threats caused by nature and those caused by human activity.
units.task: Define natural threats (e.g., heavy rainfall) and anthropogenic threats (e.g., trash blocking drains, deforestation). Show contrasting images of both types.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally state the difference between biotic and abiotic components.
units.task: Introduce the concepts of biotic and abiotic components. Show a tray of mixed items (rocks, soil, water, leaves, twigs, plastic insects) and model how to classify them into two distinct groups on the board.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can name the five interactions and give a basic definition for each.
units.task: Introduce the five ecological interactions (predation, competition, mutualism, commensalism, parasitism) using a slide presentation with clear, relatable examples for each.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can state the difference between an animal's habitat and its niche.
units.task: Define habitat (address) and niche (job). Read a short text about a local bird aloud, pausing to highlight its habitat in one color and its niche in another color on the projector.

units.mastery_criterion: Recognizes that the Earth's axis is tilted at 23 degrees and maintains this orientation throughout its orbit.
units.task: Use a globe to show the 23-degree tilt and walk it around a central light source, ensuring the tilt constantly points in the same direction.

units.mastery_criterion: Accurately draws and names the phases based on the model's shadows.
units.task: Use a foam ball on a stick and a stationary light source to model and draw the 8 moon phases.

units.mastery_criterion: Identifies Earth at center for geocentric and Sun at center for heliocentric.
units.task: Construct a Venn diagram comparing geocentric and heliocentric models after a brief lecture.

units.mastery_criterion: Defines asteroids as rocky, comets as icy, and distinguishes meteoroids, meteors, and meteorites by location.
units.task: Create a foldable defining asteroids, comets, meteoroids, meteors, and meteorites, emphasizing the location change for the last three.

units.mastery_criterion: Comic strip shows collision, debris ring, and Moon formation.
units.task: Read a text about the giant impact hypothesis and create a three-panel comic strip showing the event.

units.mastery_criterion: Categorizes all 8 planets correctly based on density and composition data.
units.task: Analyze data cards of the 8 planets (including density and composition) to discover the pattern and sort them into rocky and gas giant groups.

units.mastery_criterion: Explains natural satellites are celestial bodies and artificial are human-made.
units.task: Draw a natural satellite and an artificial satellite orbiting Earth, labeling the differences.

units.mastery_criterion: Associates Apollo 11 with the Moon landing and Voyager with outer planets.
units.task: Create a timeline of space exploration highlighting Apollo 11 and the Voyager probes.

units.mastery_criterion: Correctly labels 5 layers and describes the core's energy production.
units.task: Draw and label the Sun's layers on a poster board, then write a description of the core.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can state the direction of blood flow for arteries and veins.
units.task: Introduce arteries and veins. Spend 20 minutes explaining that arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins carry blood to the heart. Spend 25 minutes drawing a simplified circulatory loop on the board, using red for arteries and blue for veins (noting this is a pedagogical convention).

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly labels the mouth, esophagus, stomach, and intestines in order.
units.task: Introduce the digestive system organs using a large wall diagram. Spend 15 minutes tracing the path of food from the mouth, through the esophagus, to the stomach and intestines. Spend 20 minutes having students create their own labeled diagrams in their notebooks. Spend 15 minutes discussing the basic function of each organ (mouth for chewing, esophagus for transit, stomach for mixing, intestines for absorption).

units.mastery_criterion: Student can explain that kidneys filter waste from the blood.
units.task: Introduce the kidneys as filters. Spend 20 minutes explaining how blood passes through the kidneys, which remove waste to form urine. Spend 30 minutes demonstrating filtration by pouring a mixture of water and sand through a coffee filter, comparing the filter to a kidney.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly labels oxygen entering and carbon dioxide exiting the nose/mouth.
units.task: Introduce respiratory gases. Spend 15 minutes explaining that humans breathe in oxygen and breathe out carbon dioxide. Spend 15 minutes drawing a large face on the board with arrows indicating gas exchange. Spend 10 minutes having students copy the diagram and label the gases.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can point to the correct organs on the diagram when named.
units.task: Use an anatomical diagram to introduce the female reproductive system. Point out and explain the location of the ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, and vagina.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can point to the correct organs on the diagram when named.
units.task: Use an anatomical diagram to introduce the male reproductive system. Point out and explain the location of the testes, vas deferens, urethra, and penis.

units.mastery_criterion: Silhouette includes the brain in the head, spinal cord down the back, and nerves branching to limbs, color-coded correctly.
units.task: Project a diagram of the nervous system. Explain the central (brain, spinal cord) and peripheral (nerves) parts. Have students trace a human silhouette on large paper and draw the brain, spinal cord, and nerves in different colors.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally repeat the names of the 5 major bones and 3 joints when pointed to on the poster.
units.task: Introduce the human skeleton using a large anatomical poster. Point out and name the skull, ribs, spine, femur, humerus, and major joints (elbows, knees, shoulders). Have students repeat the names and locate the general area on their own bodies over their clothes.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can correctly pair each sense with its corresponding organ.
units.task: Introduce the five senses (sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch) and their corresponding organs (eyes, ears, nose, tongue, skin) using a large chart. Discuss how each organ helps us perceive the environment.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can list at least three appropriate care practices.
units.task: Discuss the importance of hygiene and care for the reproductive system. Brainstorm a list of care practices (e.g., daily bathing, clean underwear) and write them on the board.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can replicate the calculation 100W x 2h = 200Wh on their whiteboard.
units.task: Direct instruction on the formula: Power (Watts) x Time (hours) = Energy Consumption (Watt-hours). Walk through an example using a 100W bulb left on for 2 hours.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can point to the fulcrum, effort, and load on the physical ruler model for a 1st class lever.
units.task: Demonstrate the three classes of levers using a ruler, an eraser (fulcrum), and coins (load/effort). Show how moving the components changes the class (1st, 2nd, 3rd).

units.mastery_criterion: Student can point to and name at least two simple machines within the manual can opener.
units.task: Examine a manual can opener as a class. Guide students to identify the different simple machines that make it up (levers for the handles, wedge for the cutter, wheel and axle for the turner).

units.mastery_criterion: Students can point to the correct kcal value on the table for a given food item.
units.task: Explain how to read a nutritional table. Model calculating the total kilocalories of a sample meal by finding each item on the table, writing down its kcal value, and summing them up on the board.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can identify the correct order of the mapped stages.
units.task: Define a supply chain. Map the supply chain of a tomato on the board, from growing/harvesting, to transportation, to selling at a market, to purchasing at home.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can identify the gas release as the cause of the simulated eruption pressure.
units.task: Demonstrate the baking soda and vinegar volcano. Explicitly explain that the bubbles are carbon dioxide gas being released, simulating volcanic pressure, not actual magma thermodynamics.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can identify hazard symbols and explain basic vulnerability based on location.
units.task: Introduce community risk maps. Explain map symbols for hazards (steep slopes, flood zones) and resources (safe zones). Model how to evaluate which area is more vulnerable by pointing to map features.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can identify the producer, consumer, and decomposer in the modeled chain.
units.task: Explain producers, consumers, and decomposers. Use large picture cards on the board to model building a simple food chain, explicitly drawing arrows to show the direction of energy flow.

units.mastery_criterion: Explains that rotation causes day/night and translation with tilt causes seasons, including local wet/dry seasons.
units.task: Use a globe and a flashlight to model day and night, then walk the globe around the light to model seasons, discussing how this creates the wet and dry seasons in the supplied location.

units.mastery_criterion: Explains how the distance of the moon affects the size of the umbra and the resulting duration of a solar eclipse.
units.task: Use flashlights and different sized balls at varying distances to observe how the shadow cone (umbra/penumbra) changes size, relating it to eclipse duration.

units.mastery_criterion: Calculates steps and recognizes outer planets are much farther apart.
units.task: Walk a scale model of the solar system on the school field using 1 step = 0.4 AU.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can locate their pulse and record their resting heart rate.
units.task: Introduce the link between exercise and circulation. Spend 20 minutes teaching students how to find their pulse on their wrist or neck. Spend 30 minutes having them measure their resting pulse for one minute and recording it, discussing what the pulse represents.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can verbally distinguish between physical breakdown and substance transformation.
units.task: Demonstrate mechanical vs. chemical digestion. Spend 15 minutes crushing a cracker (mechanical). Spend 15 minutes placing a cracker in water and another in vinegar to observe changes (chemical model). Spend 30 minutes discussing how crushing changes size but not substance, while the liquid changes the substance's properties.

units.mastery_criterion: Identifies full moon.
units.task: Identify the moon phase if the Earth is directly between the Sun and the Moon.

units.mastery_criterion: Rejects the exact-intake inference and names a missing variable or observation.
units.task: Use a fictional written observation, not a biological sample. Evaluate whether one urine-color observation establishes an exact water intake, identify the missing evidence and explain the limit of the conclusion.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies pulling as inspiration and pushing as expiration.
units.task: Demonstrate lung mechanics using a pre-made bottle-and-balloon model. Spend 20 minutes showing how pulling the bottom membrane inflates the inner balloons (inspiration) and pushing deflates them (expiration). Spend 40 minutes letting students take turns manipulating the model and describing what they feel and see.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can verbally explain that blood connects the other systems by transporting materials.
units.task: Introduce the circulatory system as a transport network. Spend 20 minutes reviewing the functions of the lungs, intestines, and kidneys. Spend 40 minutes drawing a large map on the board showing blood picking up oxygen (lungs) and nutrients (intestines), and dropping off waste (kidneys).

units.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally define fertilization and menstruation and state where they occur.
units.task: Explain the basic processes of fertilization (meeting of ovocyte and male gamete in the oviducts) and menstruation (shedding of the endometrium from the uterus if no fertilization occurs) using simple, age-appropriate diagrams.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify which system each organ belongs to during the class discussion.
units.task: Create a large two-column chart on the board (Male / Female). Discuss each organ learned previously and have the class decide which column it belongs in, writing them down.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can point to the correct areas on a diagram when the lobes and cerebellum are named.
units.task: Project a diagram of the brain and introduce the frontal, parietal, occipital, and temporal lobes, as well as the cerebellum. Explain their locations and have students point to the approximate areas on their own heads.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally classify a given joint as immobile, semi-mobile, or mobile.
units.task: Introduce the three types of joints (immobile, semi-mobile, mobile) using a presentation and physical demonstrations. Have students move their own bodies to feel the difference between mobile joints (knees, elbows) and semi-mobile joints (spine), and point to immobile joints (skull).

units.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally explain the sequence of the message passing from skin to brain.
units.task: Explain the sensory pathway. Conduct a whole-class role-play where students act as the skin, nerves, spinal cord, and brain, passing a message (a ball) from the 'skin' to the 'brain' when a stimulus is introduced.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can point to their elbow and identify it as the fulcrum when performing a bicep curl motion.
units.task: Guide students through physical movements (nodding head, standing on tiptoes, bending arm). Explain how bones act as lever arms and joints as fulcrums.

units.mastery_criterion: Student states that moving the fulcrum closer to the load makes it easier to lift.
units.task: Conduct an experiment using a sturdy ruler on a pencil fulcrum. Students try lifting a heavy book by pressing the other end, moving the fulcrum closer to and further from the book to feel the difference in required effort.

units.mastery_criterion: Correct comparison and difference; explicitly avoids an individual food or exercise prescription.
units.task: Use teacher-provided fictional energy-use records for two activities over equal time intervals. Compare the estimates, calculate a difference and explain why the records do not prescribe exercise or food choices for individual children.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can state one reason why an imported product has a longer supply chain.
units.task: Compare the supply chain of a local mango with an imported apple. Discuss how distance adds links to the chain, requiring more transportation, fuel, and time.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally explain that removing one species affects both its predators and its prey.
units.task: Model a food web using students holding strings connecting them as different organisms. Ask what happens if one student (e.g., the grasshopper) drops their strings, and trace the impact on predators and prey.

units.mastery_criterion: Defines precession as slow change in orientation and nutation as periodic wobble caused by external gravity.
units.task: Demonstrate precession and nutation using a spinning top, then define the terms in notebooks, explicitly discussing how the gravitational pull of the Sun and Moon causes Earth's nutation.

units.mastery_criterion: Student predicts that breathing rate will increase with exercise due to oxygen demand.
units.task: Introduce the link between exercise and respiration. Spend 15 minutes discussing why the body needs oxygen. Spend 20 minutes having students count their breaths for one minute while sitting. Spend 15 minutes discussing what they expect to happen if they run.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally link the hormones to the correct biological sex and state their general purpose.
units.task: Direct instruction explaining that puberty involves bodily changes caused by sex hormones. Introduce Testosterone (primarily male) and Estrogen/Progesterone (primarily female). Discuss their role in initiating physical changes.

units.mastery_criterion: Students successfully assemble the model and can make the cardboard bend by pulling the string.
units.task: Guide students step-by-step to build a mechanical model of an arm using two pieces of cardboard joined by a brass fastener (joint) and a string attached to one piece (muscle). Demonstrate how pulling the string moves the cardboard.

units.mastery_criterion: Students contribute to a class chart detailing the step-by-step integration of the three systems.
units.task: Present a scenario: catching a falling object. Discuss as a class how the eyes, brain, nerves, muscles, and bones work together. Model how to write a logical prediction of this coordinated response.

units.mastery_criterion: Student decides to place the fulcrum near the load and justifies it by mentioning the increased distance between fulcrum and effort.
units.task: Present a scenario where a heavy box needs to be lifted with a plank. Ask the student to decide where to place the rock (fulcrum) to make it easiest to lift, and justify their choice using the law of the lever.

units.mastery_criterion: Student draws the fulcrum immediately next to the 50kg weight and writes that this reduces the required effort.
units.task: Flash diagram task: Students are given a blank lever template and must quickly draw the setup (load, fulcrum, effort) that makes lifting a 50kg weight the easiest, justifying the fulcrum placement.

units.mastery_criterion: Paragraph explicitly references the number of links or distance as the cause for increased resources/time.
units.task: Students analyze two provided supply chain diagrams (one local, one imported) and write a paragraph contrasting their resource use and time.

units.mastery_criterion: Correct identification of safe/unsafe practices with justifications referencing germ transfer.
units.task: Students read 3 short scenarios about food preparation in a kitchen. They must identify which scenarios are safe or unsafe regarding cross-contamination and write a justification for each.

units.mastery_criterion: Students justify why one location is more vulnerable than another based on specific map features.
units.task: Students look at a provided community risk map. They must decide which house (A or B) is more vulnerable to a landslide and write a paragraph justifying their choice using map symbols.

units.mastery_criterion: Students create a map with clear symbols and logically justify vulnerability based on their placement.
units.task: Students work in groups to create a simple risk map of a fictional town. They must place houses in different zones and write a justification for which house is most vulnerable to a specific threat.

units.mastery_criterion: Students consistently use map evidence (symbols, topography) to justify their vulnerability assessments.
units.task: Provide students with three different risk maps. For each map, they must answer a scenario question (e.g., 'If heavy rain falls, is the school or the hospital more vulnerable?') and justify their answer using map evidence.

units.mastery_criterion: Students quickly and accurately assess vulnerability and provide verbal justification.
units.task: Review activity: Project a new risk map on the board. Ask rapid-fire questions about vulnerability. Students write 'A' or 'B' on mini-whiteboards and hold them up, then randomly select students to justify verbally.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly match scenarios to outcomes and provide logical written justifications.
units.task: Matching game: Students match scenario cards (e.g., 'House near a deforested steep slope') with vulnerability outcome cards (e.g., 'High risk of landslide'). They must write one sentence justifying each match.

units.mastery_criterion: Students provide a logical prediction supported by evidence of energy flow disruption.
units.task: Students explain in writing what would happen to the frog and grass populations if all grasshoppers were removed from a provided food chain diagram.

units.mastery_criterion: Students provide a logical prediction supported by evidence of energy flow disruption.
units.task: Students analyze a diagram of a local food web. They must write a short paragraph predicting what would happen to two specific populations if a disease wiped out the primary consumer.

units.mastery_criterion: Students accurately track the cascading effects of species removal on their game boards.
units.task: Students play a board game where event cards remove certain species from their ecosystem board. They must calculate and record the resulting population changes based on game rules.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly predict the increase in prey population and justify it.
units.task: Review activity: Present a new scenario where a predator is overhunted. Students must quickly sketch the resulting changes in the food chain and justify their sketch to a partner.

units.mastery_criterion: Students consistently identify the correct ecological consequence of missing organisms.
units.task: Flashcard review: Students are shown 'What if?' cards regarding missing organisms and must write down the immediate consequence on a mini-whiteboard, holding it up for teacher check.

units.mastery_criterion: Correctly annotates the diagram showing the closer moon creates a larger umbra and justifies that this leads to a longer solar eclipse.
units.task: Given a visual diagram showing two moons at different distances from a planet, annotate the diagram to show their shadow cones (umbras) and write a justification for which moon causes a longer solar eclipse.

units.mastery_criterion: Correctly deduces that the closer moon creates a larger shadow cone and longer eclipses.
units.task: Work through a scenario of a hypothetical planet with two moons at different distances, answering questions about eclipse frequency and duration based on shadow geometry.

units.mastery_criterion: Identifies quarter phase and justifies based on viewing angle.
units.task: Predict the moon phase for a 90-degree alignment diagram and justify the answer.

units.mastery_criterion: Correctly shades the phases for 4 different alignments.
units.task: Given diagrams of Sun-Earth-Moon alignments, predict and shade in the visible moon phase.

units.mastery_criterion: Student connects increased physical activity to an increased heart rate to supply nutrients and oxygen.
units.task: Students are given a data table showing a person's heart rate at rest and after running. They must write a paragraph explaining why the number of beats per minute changed, referencing oxygen and nutrients.

units.mastery_criterion: Student records a higher active pulse and justifies it by the need to transport substances faster.
units.task: Test the exercise-circulation link. Spend 20 minutes having students do jumping jacks for one minute, then immediately measure their pulse. Spend 40 minutes comparing this to their resting pulse and writing an explanation of why the heart beats faster (to deliver oxygen/nutrients).

units.mastery_criterion: Student justifies why breathing rate and air volume exchange increase after physical exertion.
units.task: Students are given a scenario comparing a person sitting and a person running. They must predict which person will displace more water in a spirometer model and justify the prediction using the body's need for oxygen.

units.mastery_criterion: Student graphs the data and justifies the increase by stating the body needs more oxygen during exercise.
units.task: Test the exercise-respiration link. Spend 20 minutes having students jog in place for two minutes, then immediately count their breaths for one minute. Spend 40 minutes graphing the resting vs. active breath counts and writing a justification for the difference based on oxygen need.

units.mastery_criterion: Student explains how blood acts as the vehicle moving nutrients, oxygen, and waste to their correct locations.
units.task: Students draw a simple diagram showing the heart, lungs, intestines, and kidneys, draw arrows showing what blood picks up and drops off, and write a sentence justifying why the circulatory system is like a delivery truck.

units.mastery_criterion: Poster accurately shows oxygen/nutrients being picked up and waste being dropped off.
units.task: Create an integration poster. Spend 15 minutes planning a diagram showing the heart, lungs, intestines, and kidneys. Spend 45 minutes drawing the organs and adding arrows with labels showing what blood picks up and drops off at each location.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly navigates the stations, picking up and dropping off the correct tokens.
units.task: Role-play the transport system. Spend 20 minutes setting up stations (Lungs, Intestines, Kidneys, Cells) and assigning roles (Blood cells carrying tokens). Spend 40 minutes running the simulation where 'blood' picks up 'oxygen' (blue tokens) and 'nutrients' (green tokens), delivers them to 'cells', and takes 'waste' (red tokens) to 'kidneys'.

units.mastery_criterion: Rejects the exact-intake inference and names a missing variable or observation.
units.task: Use a fictional written observation, not a biological sample. Evaluate whether one urine-color observation establishes an exact water intake, identify the missing evidence and explain the limit of the conclusion.

units.mastery_criterion: Rejects the exact-intake inference and names a missing variable or observation.
units.task: Use a fictional written observation, not a biological sample. Evaluate whether one urine-color observation establishes an exact water intake, identify the missing evidence and explain the limit of the conclusion.

units.mastery_criterion: Response includes sensory input (eyes), brain processing, and muscle-bone interaction for movement.
units.task: Read the scenario: You see a ball flying towards your face. Write a short paragraph predicting how your nervous, muscular, and skeletal systems will work together to catch or dodge it.

units.mastery_criterion: Paragraph includes sensory input from the foot, brain processing, and muscle-bone interaction to lift the foot.
units.task: Students write a paragraph predicting the coordinated response of the nervous, muscular, and skeletal systems when a person steps on a sharp stone barefoot.

units.mastery_criterion: Briefly mentions nerves detecting heat, brain processing, and muscles pulling arm bones away.
units.task: Quick write: Explain the system coordination that happens when you accidentally touch a hot plate and pull your hand away.

units.mastery_criterion: Flowchart shows ears -> nerves -> brain -> nerves -> neck muscles -> neck bones.
units.task: Draw a quick flowchart showing the system coordination when you hear a loud noise and turn your head to look.

units.mastery_criterion: Student proposes unplugging the devices and justifies it by mentioning phantom load or unnecessary energy consumption while off.
units.task: Read a scenario where a family leaves their microwave and TV plugged in all day while at work. Propose one action they should take to lower their energy bill and explain why it works.

units.mastery_criterion: Student proposes a valid action and justifies it by mentioning energy consumed while off.
units.task: Students write a short letter to a family member proposing one specific energy-saving habit (e.g., unplugging the TV at night) and justifying it using the concept of phantom load.

units.mastery_criterion: Student draws the fulcrum close to the crate and writes that increasing the distance from effort to fulcrum reduces the required force.
units.task: Students design a lever system on paper to lift a heavy crate. They must draw the optimal fulcrum placement and write a short paragraph justifying their choice based on the distance between effort and fulcrum.

units.mastery_criterion: Student identifies a plugged-in device and verbally justifies unplugging it to stop phantom load.
units.task: Role-play: Students act as 'energy auditors' inspecting the classroom. They identify devices plugged in but not in use, recommend unplugging them, and explain why to the class.

units.mastery_criterion: Student selects Setup A and justifies it by noting the longer distance between the effort and the fulcrum.
units.task: Students compare two illustrations of lever setups (Setup A has fulcrum near load, Setup B has fulcrum near effort). They predict which requires less effort and write a justification using evidence from the law of the lever.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies the sequence: mechanical (cranking) -> electrical -> sound/light.
units.task: Students examine a hand-crank radio or flashlight (or a video of one if unavailable) and trace the energy transformations from human mechanical energy to the final output.

units.mastery_criterion: Poster includes a clear action and a scientifically accurate justification regarding energy waste.
units.task: Students create an energy-saving campaign poster for the school, featuring a rule (e.g., 'Unplug chargers!') and a scientific justification based on energy consumption.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly plots the data points and writes a conclusion stating that as distance from effort to fulcrum increases, effort required decreases.
units.task: Students are given a hypothetical data table showing effort required at different fulcrum distances. They graph the data and write a conclusion about the relationship between distance and effort.

units.mastery_criterion: Student marks the end of the crowbar furthest from the crate and explains it maximizes distance from the fulcrum.
units.task: Quick review scenario: Show a picture of a person using a crowbar to open a crate. Ask students to mark an 'X' where the person should hold the crowbar to use the least effort, and write one sentence explaining why.

units.mastery_criterion: Explanation explicitly references the number of links or distance in the supply chain as the cause.
units.task: Students write an explanation of why an apple imported from another country might cost more and take longer to arrive than a mango grown in their town, using the concept of supply chain links.

units.mastery_criterion: Identifies the transfer of germs/contamination from raw to cooked food as the reason.
units.task: Students write a response to the prompt: 'Why is it important to use a different knife for cutting raw chicken and slicing cooked bread? Justify your answer.'

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify and log at least two natural and two anthropogenic threats.
units.task: Students walk around the school perimeter to conduct a threat assessment, logging potential natural and anthropogenic threats on a clipboard.

units.mastery_criterion: Students successfully execute the reaction and observe the gas release.
units.task: In small groups, students perform the volcano simulation themselves, varying the amount of baking soda to observe changes in the amount of gas produced.

units.mastery_criterion: Diagrams accurately represent the simulation components, specifically highlighting the gas release.
units.task: Students draw a detailed, cross-sectional diagram of the volcano simulation they performed, labeling the liquid mixture, the container, and specifically drawing and labeling the escaping carbon dioxide gas bubbles.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly list 5 biotic and 5 abiotic items from their immediate environment.
units.task: Students go on a guided walk around the schoolyard to observe the environment. They carry a clipboard and draw or write 5 biotic and 5 abiotic items they find, then return to class to share.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly sort at least 8 out of 10 cut-out items onto the T-chart.
units.task: Provide students with nature magazines. They must cut out 10 pictures of environmental items and glue them onto a T-chart labeled Biotic and Abiotic.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly label 4 biotic and 4 abiotic components in their diorama.
units.task: Students create a diorama of a local ecosystem using a shoebox, explicitly labeling at least 4 biotic and 4 abiotic components.

units.mastery_criterion: Students build a valid food chain with at least three trophic levels and correct directional arrows.
units.task: Using provided cards of local organisms, students independently arrange them into a food chain and draw arrows showing energy flow on their assessment paper.

units.mastery_criterion: Students build valid food chains with correct directional arrows indicating energy flow.
units.task: Students work in pairs with sets of organism cards. They must arrange the cards into at least three different valid food chains and draw the energy flow arrows on a recording sheet.

units.mastery_criterion: The mobile accurately represents a food chain sequence.
units.task: Students create a 3D food chain mobile using paper cups, string, and drawings of organisms. They must hang them in order of energy flow, from producer at the top to decomposer at the bottom.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly label 4 out of 5 interaction scenarios.
units.task: Students read 5 short scenarios of animal interactions on a worksheet and label each with the correct ecological term.

units.mastery_criterion: Students accurately portray and identify the ecological interactions.
units.task: Students work in small groups to act out short, silent skits representing one of the five interactions. The rest of the class must guess which interaction is being portrayed.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly sort at least 8 out of 10 scenario cards.
units.task: Students are given 10 scenario cards describing animal interactions. They must sort them into five labeled envelopes corresponding to the five interaction types.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly separate habitat and niche information for at least 3 out of 4 animals.
units.task: Students receive a set of animal profile cards. They must read each profile and fill out a graphic organizer separating the habitat details from the niche details for each animal.

units.mastery_criterion: The poster clearly distinguishes the physical location from the ecological role.
units.task: Students choose a local animal and create a 'Job Application' poster for it, clearly stating its 'address' (habitat) and its 'skills/duties' (niche) in the ecosystem.

units.mastery_criterion: Identifies rotation for day/night and explicitly links translation plus axial tilt to the specific changing seasons in El Salvador.
units.task: Write a paragraph explaining why it is night in the supplied location when it is day in Japan, and how Earth's translation and tilt cause the supplied location's specific location to experience wet and dry seasons instead of four temperate seasons.

units.mastery_criterion: Accurately describes the time difference due to Earth's rotation and the seasonal difference due to translation and tilt.
units.task: Write a short story from the perspective of a person in the supplied location experiencing the wet season and a person in Japan experiencing a different season, explaining the Earth's position.

units.mastery_criterion: Answers all three questions correctly based on Earth's movements.
units.task: Answer three flashcard questions about what causes day, night, and seasons.

units.mastery_criterion: Correctly sorts the unknown planets and justifies using the density data.
units.task: Classify four unknown planets as rocky or gas giants based on a provided data table of their densities, and justify the choices.

units.mastery_criterion: Accurately classifies exoplanets using density comparisons (rock-like vs gas-like).
units.task: Review a table of hypothetical exoplanets with raw data (density, radius) linked to familiar materials (e.g., 'density similar to rock' vs 'density similar to air/water') and classify them as rocky or gas giants, writing a justification for each.

units.mastery_criterion: Correctly calculates 3 steps.
units.task: Calculate how many steps are needed to represent a planet 1.2 AU away (1 step = 0.4 AU).

units.mastery_criterion: Correctly calculates the number of steps for at least three planets and accurately identifies the largest gap between consecutive planets.
units.task: Calculate the scale distances (in steps) for different planets and compare them to determine which planets are closest together and which are farthest apart in the model.

units.mastery_criterion: Student differentiates between physical breakdown (mechanical) and substance transformation (chemical) with correct justification.
units.task: Students observe a video or live demonstration of paper being torn (mechanical) and paper being burned (chemical - modeled via video only for safety). They must write a paragraph classifying each and relating it to human digestion.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies crushing as mechanical and dissolving as chemical digestion in their written comparison.
units.task: Students perform their own digestion modeling. Spend 20 minutes crushing chalk (mechanical). Spend 20 minutes placing chalk in vinegar (chemical). Spend 20 minutes writing a comparison of the two processes in their notebooks, identifying which represents mechanical and which represents chemical digestion.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly sorts at least 8 out of 10 scenario cards.
units.task: Quick recall activity: Spend 10 minutes reviewing previous notes. Spend 20 minutes sorting 10 scenario cards (e.g., 'chewing an apple', 'saliva breaking down starch') into 'Mechanical' or 'Chemical' digestion piles.

units.mastery_criterion: Student manipulates a model to demonstrate how volume changes cause air to enter or leave the simulated lungs.
units.task: Students are given a bottle-and-balloon model one by one. They must demonstrate inspiration and expiration, and verbally explain which action represents which respiratory movement.

units.mastery_criterion: Student successfully builds a working model and writes that expanding the space pulls air in.
units.task: Students build their own simple lung models. Spend 30 minutes assembling a model using a plastic cup, a straw, and two balloons. Spend 30 minutes testing the models and writing down how the volume changes affect the air inside.

units.mastery_criterion: Student accurately performs their role in the sequence of inspiration and expiration.
units.task: Role-play respiratory mechanics. Spend 20 minutes assigning roles (diaphragm, lungs, air). Spend 40 minutes practicing and performing a physical representation where the 'diaphragm' moves down, the 'lungs' expand, and 'air' rushes in, then reversing the process.

units.mastery_criterion: All 6 organs are placed in the correct column.
units.task: Sort the following organs into a two-column table for Male and Female: Uterus, Testes, Ovaries, Prostate, Vagina, Vas Deferens.

units.mastery_criterion: Testosterone matches Male. Estrogen/Progesterone match Female. Sentence states they cause bodily changes during puberty.
units.task: Match the hormone to the biological sex it primarily affects during puberty, and write one sentence explaining why these hormones are important.

units.mastery_criterion: Student explicitly states that the muscle (string) pulls the bone (cardboard) to create movement at the joint.
units.task: Using the previously built cardboard and string model of an arm, pull the string and write a short description of what happens to the cardboard pieces and how this relates to real muscles and bones.

units.mastery_criterion: Sequence strictly follows: Skin touches hot surface -> Nerves detect heat -> Signal travels to spinal cord and brain -> Brain registers pain.
units.task: Order the provided cards to show what happens when you touch a hot surface, from the moment of touch to the brain registering pain.

units.mastery_criterion: All card sets are ordered correctly from stimulus to brain.
units.task: Students work in small groups to sort sets of cards representing different sensory scenarios (e.g., smelling a flower, hearing a bell) into the correct pathway order.

units.mastery_criterion: Poster accurately separates male and female organs into distinct columns.
units.task: Students create a comparative poster with two columns, drawing one key organ for each system and listing the other organs below it.

units.mastery_criterion: Students explain that pulling the string simulates muscle contraction pulling on bones to bend the fingers.
units.task: Students create a mechanical hand model by taping cut straws (bones) onto a paper hand outline and threading string (tendons/muscles) through them. Pulling the strings bends the paper fingers.

units.mastery_criterion: Matches are made correctly, showing the relationship between hormones, sex, and puberty.
units.task: Students complete a matching activity linking 'Testosterone' and 'Estrogen/Progesterone' to 'Male' and 'Female', and linking both to 'Causes physical changes during puberty'.

units.mastery_criterion: Model demonstrates that the rubber band (muscle) must cross the joint to pull the lower stick (bone).
units.task: Students design and build a model of a leg (knee joint) using craft sticks and rubber bands, exploring how the rubber band must be positioned to pull the lower stick upward.

units.mastery_criterion: Brochure accurately names the hormones and their role in puberty.
units.task: Students create a simple, abstract informational brochure explaining what hormones are and how they trigger the changes of puberty in males and females.

units.mastery_criterion: All cards are placed in the correct box.
units.task: Students work in pairs with a deck of cards containing names of reproductive organs. They must sort them into two physical boxes labeled 'Male' and 'Female'.

units.mastery_criterion: Storyboard panels are in the correct chronological order showing the pathway to the brain.
units.task: Students draw a 4-panel storyboard illustrating the sequence of events when a person touches a cold ice cube, showing the stimulus, nerve transmission, spinal cord routing, and brain processing.

units.mastery_criterion: Majority of the class holds up the correct color card for each organ.
units.task: Teacher holds up a flashcard with an organ name. Students hold up a blue card for male or a yellow card for female.

units.mastery_criterion: Lines correctly connect organs to the appropriate biological sex.
units.task: Students complete a quick worksheet where they draw a line connecting the organ name to either a 'Male' or 'Female' icon.

units.mastery_criterion: Student provides the correct numerical answer (400) and unit (Wh).
units.task: A television uses 100 W of power. If it is turned on for 4 hours, what is the total energy consumption in Watt-hours?

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly labels the three components and identifies it as a second-class lever.
units.task: Show a diagram of a wheelbarrow. Ask the student to label the fulcrum, effort, and load, and state which class of lever it is.

units.mastery_criterion: Student identifies at least two different simple machines and accurately locates them on the bicycle.
units.task: Show a picture of a bicycle. Ask the student to name two simple machines found in it and point out where they are.

units.mastery_criterion: Student accurately maps the toes as the fulcrum, the ankle/body weight as the load, and the calf muscle pulling up as the effort.
units.task: Ask the student to stand on their tiptoes and then draw a simple diagram of their foot, labeling the fulcrum, effort, and load.

units.mastery_criterion: Student states that electrical energy is transformed into mechanical (kinetic) energy.
units.task: Describe the energy transformation that occurs when you turn on an electric fan.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly calculates the Watt-hours for at least 4 out of 5 appliances.
units.task: Students calculate the daily Watt-hours for a list of 5 appliances, given their power ratings in Watts and daily usage in hours.

units.mastery_criterion: Student constructs three models with the fulcrum, effort, and load in the correct relative positions for each class.
units.task: Students build paper models of the three lever classes using cardboard strips and brass fasteners, labeling the parts on each model.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies and locates at least three different simple machines on the bicycle diagram.
units.task: Students analyze a detailed diagram of a bicycle, locating and naming the simple machines present (e.g., wheel and axle, levers for brakes, screws).

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly circles the knee, elbow/shoulder, and neck joints as fulcrums in the respective drawings.
units.task: Students draw stick figures performing three actions (kicking a ball, lifting a box, looking up). They must circle the joint acting as the fulcrum in each action.

units.mastery_criterion: Student accurately identifies electrical energy as the input and the correct output energy (heat, light/sound, mechanical) for all three appliances.
units.task: Students create an 'energy chain' poster for three common household appliances (e.g., toaster, television, washing machine), identifying the input and output energy forms.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly multiplies daily consumption by 7 to find the weekly total.
units.task: Word problems: Students solve multi-step problems, such as finding the total weekly energy consumption of a television used 3 hours a day.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly labels the three components and identifies the lever class for at least two of the three tools.
units.task: Analyze diagrams of a wheelbarrow, scissors, and tweezers. Students draw arrows to indicate the fulcrum, effort, and load, and state the lever class for each.

units.mastery_criterion: Student lists at least two valid simple machines for their assigned complex machine.
units.task: Invention breakdown: Provide pictures of large complex machines (e.g., a construction crane, a mechanical clock). Students list the simple machine parts they can identify visually.

units.mastery_criterion: Student accurately maps the three lever components to the arm curl movement.
units.task: In pairs, one student holds a book in their hand and curls their arm. The partner observes and maps the effort (bicep), fulcrum (elbow), and load (book).

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly matches at least 8 out of 10 appliance cards to their energy transformation.
units.task: Matching game: Students match cards showing appliances to cards describing their specific energy transformation (e.g., Blender -> Electrical to Mechanical).

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly calculates total wattage (300W) and multiplies by hours (6) to get 1800Wh.
units.task: Students estimate the energy consumption for a hypothetical school day by calculating the Wh of 10 classroom lights (30W each) left on for 6 hours.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly sorts at least three tools into their proper lever class based on component location.
units.task: Students are given a mixed bag of safe, everyday tools (e.g., tongs, bottle opener, pliers). They must test them, locate the fulcrum, effort, and load, and sort them by lever class.

units.mastery_criterion: Student's drawing clearly incorporates and correctly labels three distinct simple machines working together.
units.task: Students design a hypothetical complex machine on paper (e.g., a machine to feed a pet) that must incorporate at least three different simple machines, labeling each one.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly labels the three components on the jaw diagram.
units.task: Students analyze a diagram of a human jaw chewing food. They must label the temporomandibular joint as the fulcrum, the jaw muscles as effort, and the food as the load.

units.mastery_criterion: Correct mathematical sum matching the specific values in the provided table.
units.task: Students use a provided nutritional table to calculate the total kilocalories in a specific meal consisting of 1 tortilla, 3 tablespoons of beans, and 1 cup of atol.

units.mastery_criterion: Chart includes title, labeled axes, correct scale, and accurate bar heights.
units.task: Using a provided data table showing how many students ate local vs. imported fruits, students draw a bar chart with labeled axes and a title.

units.mastery_criterion: Identifies the zero/unit error and states a matching correction.
units.task: Inspect fictional diagrams of a model measured with a ruler and a scale. Find a missing unit or non-zero starting point, describe its effect on the record, and correct the recording procedure.

units.mastery_criterion: Correct comparison and difference; explicitly avoids an individual food or exercise prescription.
units.task: Use teacher-provided fictional energy-use records for two activities over equal time intervals. Compare the estimates, calculate a difference and explain why the records do not prescribe exercise or food choices for individual children.

units.mastery_criterion: Flowchart includes growing/harvesting, transportation, selling, and purchasing/preparing in a logical sequence.
units.task: Students draw a flowchart showing the steps a tomato takes from being grown on a farm to being eaten at home, labeling each step.

units.mastery_criterion: Accurate mathematical sums matching the table values for all three menus.
units.task: Students receive three hypothetical daily menus and a nutritional reference table. They must calculate the total kilocalories for each menu, showing all addition steps.

units.mastery_criterion: Chart includes title, labeled axes, correct scale, and accurate bar heights.
units.task: Students are given a data table showing hypothetical survey results of favorite local vs. imported fruits. They must construct a complete bar chart on grid paper.

units.mastery_criterion: Identifies the zero/unit error and states a matching correction.
units.task: Inspect fictional diagrams of a model measured with a ruler and a scale. Find a missing unit or non-zero starting point, describe its effect on the record, and correct the recording procedure.

units.mastery_criterion: Correct comparison and difference; explicitly avoids an individual food or exercise prescription.
units.task: Use teacher-provided fictional energy-use records for two activities over equal time intervals. Compare the estimates, calculate a difference and explain why the records do not prescribe exercise or food choices for individual children.

units.mastery_criterion: Logical sequence of at least four distinct supply chain stages glued in order.
units.task: Students receive a set of mixed cards showing the steps of a supply chain for coffee. They must sequence the cards correctly and glue them onto a flowchart template.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly calculate the total kcal for at least three flashcard meals.
units.task: Flashcard activity where students draw a card with a meal, look up the items on their reference table, and quickly calculate the total kcal on a mini-whiteboard.

units.mastery_criterion: Peer verification confirms the correct sum of kilocalories based on the table.
units.task: Students create a 5-item hypothetical meal, calculate its total kcal using the table, and then swap with a peer to verify the calculation.

units.mastery_criterion: Students accurately read the water level on a millimeter scale within a 2mm margin of error.
units.task: Students read the water level in three different simulated pluviometers (printed images) and record the measurements in millimeters.

units.mastery_criterion: Students accurately read the water level on their homemade millimeter scale.
units.task: Students build a simple pluviometer using a plastic bottle and a ruler. They pour different amounts of water into it and practice reading the measurements in millimeters.

units.mastery_criterion: Students accurately record the measurements within a 2mm margin of error.
units.task: Set up 5 stations with graduated cylinders containing different amounts of colored water. Students rotate through the stations and record the measurements in millimeters on a lab sheet.

units.mastery_criterion: Students accurately plot the millimeter measurements on a bar graph.
units.task: Students analyze a week's worth of simulated rainfall data collected in their pluviometers, graphing the daily measurements in millimeters.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify multiple threats and categorize them accurately.
units.task: Students analyze a set of photographs taken around a hypothetical town. They must identify and list all the natural and anthropogenic threats they can find in the images.

units.mastery_criterion: Students accurately highlight and categorize the threats in the text.
units.task: Students read three short case studies of different communities. For each, they must highlight natural threats in yellow and anthropogenic threats in green.

units.mastery_criterion: Students successfully execute the reaction and identify the gas bubbles as the simulated volcanic pressure in their diagram.
units.task: Students perform a micro-version of the volcano simulation individually and then draw a diagram labeling the liquid mixture and the escaping gas on their assessment sheet.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly places and labels arteries (away from heart) and veins (toward heart).
units.task: Vessel mapping activity. Spend 15 minutes reviewing the concepts. Spend 35 minutes having students trace a body outline on large paper and draw the heart, adding red yarn for arteries (away) and blue yarn for veins (toward). Spend 15 minutes labeling the yarn.

units.mastery_criterion: Student verbally explains the integration of the systems accurately without notes.
units.task: Verbal explanation recall. Spend 15 minutes having students write a short 'elevator pitch' explaining how the body systems work together. Spend 15 minutes having them present their pitch to a partner without looking at their notes.

units.mastery_criterion: At least 3 out of 4 organs are correctly labeled.
units.task: Given a diagram of the female reproductive system, label the ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, and vagina.

units.mastery_criterion: At least 3 out of 4 organs are correctly labeled.
units.task: Given a diagram of the male reproductive system, label the testes, vas deferens, urethra, and penis.

units.mastery_criterion: Drawing shows the brain in the head, connected to a spinal cord running down the center, with nerves branching out to the arms and legs.
units.task: Draw the central and peripheral nervous system on a blank human silhouette, using different colors for the brain, spinal cord, and nerves.

units.mastery_criterion: Labels placed correctly on the skull, ribs, spine, femur, and humerus. Circles placed on elbows, knees, or shoulders.
units.task: Given a blank diagram of the human skeleton, label the skull, ribs, spine, femur, humerus, and circle three joints.

units.mastery_criterion: Clay bones are placed in the correct anatomical positions on the cardboard outline.
units.task: Students use modeling clay to form the shapes of the skull, ribs, spine, femur, and humerus, placing them on a cardboard body outline. They must place small clay balls to represent the joints.

units.mastery_criterion: Diagram is accurately color-coded with a matching legend.
units.task: Students receive a detailed printed diagram of the human body and must color-code the brain red, the spinal cord blue, and the nerves yellow, then add a legend.

units.mastery_criterion: All organ names are correctly matched to their corresponding shapes.
units.task: Students play a matching game where they match the name of the female reproductive organ to a card showing its specific shape isolated from the rest of the system.

units.mastery_criterion: All organ names are correctly matched to their corresponding shapes.
units.task: Students play a matching game where they match the name of the male reproductive organ to a card showing its specific shape isolated from the rest of the system.

units.mastery_criterion: Playdough shapes roughly match the anatomical structure and are labeled correctly.
units.task: Students use playdough to create a 2D model of the female reproductive system on a paper plate, labeling the ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, and vagina with toothpick flags.

units.mastery_criterion: Playdough shapes roughly match the anatomical structure and are labeled correctly.
units.task: Students use playdough to create a 2D model of the male reproductive system on a paper plate, labeling the testes, vas deferens, urethra, and penis with toothpick flags.

units.mastery_criterion: Puzzle is assembled correctly and all required bones and joints are accurately labeled.
units.task: Students work in pairs to assemble a life-size paper skeleton puzzle on the floor, labeling the skull, ribs, spine, femur, humerus, and circling the joints with a marker.

units.mastery_criterion: Yarn is glued in the correct anatomical positions representing the three main components.
units.task: Students use different colored yarn and glue to map the brain, spinal cord, and nerves onto a cardboard body outline.
